subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF DECISION TO ESTABLISH OFFICIAL RESIDENCE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF DECISION TO ESTABLISH OFFICIAL RESIDENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, I should like to mention a subject that is in the minds of members of parliament, and, I believe, a large section of the public. My subject is a permanent home in Ottawa for Canada's prime ministers. Canada is one of the few countries that does not have an official residence for its prime minister. Most of us realize the difficulty of a prime minister, coming to Ottawa for an uncertain tenure, in obtaining the type of house suitable to the high office he holds.
Some years ago the government purchased the Edwards property, which is located on the banks of the Ottawa river adjacent to the French embassy The government purchased the property without any particular purpose in mind. At the moment it is rented to the Australian high commissioner and used as a legation. The lease on the property expires on the first of November. Today the government, acting in the absence of the Prime Minister, has decided to ask parliament to make it possible to rehabilitate the house by making provision for the cost of alterations, repairs and future maintenance. If there is no serious opposition to this program, the house will be asked, in the estimates for 1950, to provide funds for the required repairs, alterations and future maintenance of that property as a home for Canada's prime minister.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of ihe Opposition):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF DECISION TO ESTABLISH OFFICIAL RESIDENCE
speechtext:
Shortly before the opening of this sitting, Mr. Speaker, I was informed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce of. the government's decision to make arrangements for an official residence for Canada's prime ministers. I feel sure the decision is one which will meet with the general approval of the members of this house and of citizens in every part of Canada. Members of parliament know-it may not be known generally throughout the rest of the country-the extent to which the Prime Minister of Canada is called upon to receive official visitors.
Certain duties which are essential to that high office should be a part of the responsibility of the state.
I am not in a position to give any opinion as to the particular residence mentioned. I do wish to express our satisfaction that the Prime Minister will have the opportunity of carrying on his official duties and receiving official visitors in a manner more in keeping with Canada's present position in world affairs. These visits of important and distinguished visitors are no mere social engagements. They are part of world development in one of the most important periods of history. The fact that in these days Ottawa should be visited by so many of the leaders of other nations is in itself evidence of the importance that Canada has assumed in the minds of the governments of other countries. It will assist the Prime Minister of Canada, not only in receiving those important visitors but in carrying out his own heavy personal duties, to have a permanent home, where, as the elected head of the government of Canada, he can discharge his responsibilities in a manner that will be in keeping with the status of Canada in the world today.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF DECISION TO ESTABLISH OFFICIAL RESIDENCE
speechtext:
I am glad, Mr. Speaker, that the announcement was made this afternoon that a home will be provided for the prime ministers of Canada. I am also grateful to the Minister of Trade and Commerce for mentioning this matter before the opening of this sitting, because I can now speak not only for myself, but for my colleagues, whom I have had an opportunity to consult.
The house that has been chosen is beautifully situated on the Ottawa river. I am sure that visitors to Canada who are entertained there will appreciate the beauty of the city more than they would if they were housed in a hotel in the heart of the city. I know where the house is, and I know something about it. Several times since the minister spoke about this matter, I have wondered whether the government might not be well advised to build a new house, with modern conveniences, and perhaps more suitable for the purpose in mind, instead of reconditioning or rebuilding the interior of an old house. I hope the government may give some consideration to this suggestion.
I am glad that the Prime Minister is to be suitably housed; and I hope that we in this

speechtext: Will the minister make a statement explaining this proposed measure?

subtopic: CORPORATION TO TAKE OVER PROPERTY AND EQUIPMENT OF MARCONI AND CABLE AND WIRELESS LIMITED
speechtext:
Yes. I thought the proper place to make it was on second reading, but I am prepared to make it at this stage.
In a statement to the house on November 8, 1945, concerning commonwealth communications, the then acting prime minister stated that the Canadian government had indicated its willingness to nationalize external telecommunication services-in other words to acquire the overseas telecommunication facilities owned and operated in Canada by the Canadian Marconi Company, Limited, and Cable and Wireless, Limited.
I think perhaps I should here give the house a brief outline of the history of external telecommunications. The present organization of these services goes back to 1928, when the position created by the competition between the beam wireless telegraph services and the submarine cable telegraph services came under review by the Imperial Wireless and Cable Conference, 1928.
The recommendations of the conference were approved by the governments of the commonwealth, and as a result two companies were formed: one, a merger company owning practically all the shares of the old cable companies and the Marconi Wireless Telegraph Company; the other, now known as Cable and Wireless, Limited, an operating company owning all the communication assets of the merger company, certain cables previously-owned by the governments of the commonwealth, and a lease of the beam wireless stations in the United Kingdom then owned by the United Kingdom post office. At the same time there was established a communications advisory committee-now the commonwealth communications	council-a body which
included representatives of the dominion and which was given certain powers of control over policy and rates. This committee was the official means of communications between the various governments and the company.
Soon after the formation of Cable and Wireless, Limited, operating difficulties became apparent. There was serious contraction in international trade in 1930, and in addition the company had to face foreign competition, particularly from new wireless, telegraph services. These difficulties led to a review of the relationship between Cable and Wireless, Limited, and the governments of the

Overseas Telecommunication Act commonwealth, and certain changes were made in the operational and financial arrangements.
Coming down to the war years, I should mention that direct radio circuits were established between the United States and many parts of the commonwealth. Such circuits were opened on the understanding that their operation was limited to the duration of the war, but it later became evident that it would be inexpedient to close them, notwithstanding the fact that their retention would result in a loss of revenue to the commonwealth cable and radio circuits.
The problems which had arisen were *considered at the commonwealth telegraph conference held in Australia, and later by the [DOT]commonwealth communications council at a meeting in 1944. The view of the council was that the needs of the commonwealth telecommunications system were not being adequately served, and that there should be a change in the organization. Companies existed in the dominions and India; nevertheless the main instrument of commonwealth telecommunications was Cable and Wireless, Limited, a United Kingdom company owning a substantial interest in the capital of local companies. The council felt it was essential that the dominions and India should have a greater share in the administration of the commonwealth telecommunications system with a view to building it up as a whole on both cable and wireless sides. It was also felt that a company with obligations to private shareholders might not be in a position to provide a service which would fully satisfy public needs and strategic requirements.
Early in 1945 Lord Reith, on behalf of the United Kingdom government, visited the dominions and India to explain the point of view of the British government. Following these discussions the commonwealth telecommunications conference was held in London in 1945, and the conference unanimously recommended public ownership of the overseas telecommunication services of all the commonwealth governments. Pursuant to this recommendation the United Kingdom government purchased all the shares of Cable and Wireless Limited which it did not already own, and subsequently an agreement, designated as the "over-all agreement", and now known as the commonwealth telegraphs agreement, was signed in London on May 11, 1948, by representatives of each of the commonwealth governments, referred to in the agreement as the partner governments.
The agreement provided, in part, that each partner government in whose territory a local company is operating external telecommunication services shall purchase all the

shares in the local company or otherwise acquire the local company's undertaking; that for the purpose of acquiring the local assets and of operating and maintaining its external telecommunication services each partner government shall either nominate an existing department or other body or establish a public corporation having the powers necessary to carry into effect the provisions of the agreement, such agency being referred to in the agreement as "the national body"; and that for the purpose of promoting the efficiency and development of the external telecommunication services of the commonwealth there shall be established a body known as the commonwealth telecommunications board.
The functions of this board will be mainly advisory, but substantially wider than those of the commonwealth communications council which it replaces, and including: (a) the formulation of joint telecommunication policy, including rates; (b) the co-ordination and development of the wireless and cable systems of the commonwealth; (c) the co-ordination with the appropriate authorities oJ telecommunication matters affecting the defence of the commonwealth; (d) the coordination and conduct of research; (e negotiations with foreign telecommunicatior interests, if requested to undertake these bj the commonwealth governments.
Cable and Wireless, Limited, was transferred to public ownership of the Unitec Kingdom under the Cable and Wireless Act effective January 1, 1947, with the shart capital of the company transferred to th( United Kingdom government. The company will remain in being as a government-ownec company and will continue to own the asset: and operate the telecommunication service; outside the United Kingdom apart from thosi to be operated by the respective nationa bodies of the partner governments. Thi commonwealth telegraphs bill which wa presented to the United Kingdom parliamen on February 1, 1949, provides for the estab lishment of the commonwealth telecom munications board and for the transfer of th assets of Cable and Wireless, Limited, in th United Kingdom to the United Kingdon general post office, its national body, effectiv April 1, 1950.
The governments of Australia, New Zea land and South Africa have already passe the necessary legislation to establish thei national bodies. Southern Rhodesia too: over operation of its external telecommuni cation services on April 1, 1949, and Indi on January 1, 1947, while the policy of th governments in Pakistan and Ceylon has nc yet been decided.

Overseas Telecommunication Act
Canada has approved the financial arrangements under the "over-all agreement", based on the wayleave scheme as recommended by a conference of financial experts from the commonwealth countries, including Canada, held in London in October, 1947, on the understanding that final acceptance will be conditional upon acceptance by all commonwealth governments concerned.
In brief, these arrangements call for, first, each country to retain all receipts on originating traffic, less out-payments to carrier companies handling such traffic other than carriers of the national bodies; second, each national body to make payments towards the expenses of the commonwealth telecommunications board, based on the proportion of its receipts to the total net receipts of all national bodies; third, each national body to make wayleave payments to the central board towards the over-all expenses of maintaining and operating all common user cable and radio services of the commonwealth telecommunications system, based on the proportion of its net receipts to the total receipts of all national bodies.
Under the wayleave scheme, the Canadian body, namely, the proposed Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation, the establishment of which is provided for in the bill to be brought down, will, according to figures made available by the commonwealth communications council, based on 1947 traffic volume, show an annual profit of approximately $50,000. My technical officers are inclined to put this estimate at a higher figure. I might add that the financial effects of the wayleave scheme are to be reviewed by the central body immediately after figures for one year's operations are available from all national bodies.
The resolution now presented to the house can, I believe, be divided into five heads, which provide, first of all, for the establishment of a corporation to be known as the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation, which will take over the telecommunication assets of Cable and Wireless, Limited, together with those of Canadian Marconi Company, Limited.
The object, too, of the corporation will be to operate these telecommunication services not only in this country but also in cooperation and in co-ordination with other commonwealth countries. The second part of the resolution provides for funds for this purpose. As stipulated there, they are not to exceed the sum of $4,500,000. It also provides for working capital.
The third part of the resolution provides for loans which may be made to the corporation from time to time, none of which on any occasion shall exceed the sum of $100,000. The two remaining paragraphs provide, first, for losses which may be made by the corporation, such losses to be voted by parliament, and, second, for payment to the Receiver General of Canada of profits which may be made by the corporation.
If the house so desired, I would be prepared to make any further remarks when the bill is presented. I understand in the resolution stage it is not the custom to debate the measure at length, and perhaps I might limit my remarks at the present time to what I have just said.

Mr. Speaker, I realize that the action now proposed is being taken more or less to consolidate this kind of service in the commonwealth. I hope, however, that the house will look into the financial structure of these organizations and give careful attention to the balance sheets of the companies, particularly the Canadian Marconi Company, which we propose to take over.

While a government corporation ostensibly may be responsible to parliament, it always feels that it can call upon parliament or the people to cover any losses. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to call the attention of the house to one or two matters relating to this important resolution.
The war broke out in 1939, and after ten years-six of war and four of the aftermath of war-the government want to make a change, although they were satisfied during that period with the present method of external communication.
Originally there was a code. The idea of making a change started when the war broke out, because of the code used. I referred to that the other night in connection with the Statute of Westminster. Tb ere is a difference
Overseas Telecommunication Act between the old system and the new one. When the war broke out, what did they have? For two and a half years the dominions were the only countries behind the mother country, and they had a code system. The government had the right to make rules and regulations as to the code. After two and a half years of war, during which Great Britain and the dominions worked together, they decided to adopt a new code because of the entry of the United States into the conflict.
I have been reading extensively about this whole matter, and it arises out of the statute I have named. In the first place there are external communication services by other means. The radio is used extensively for external communication, so much so that there is a radiotelephone system between Canada and the old country. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the British Broadcasting Corporation have the right to make rules and regulations as to their code, and today it has been expanded.
You will notice the change in the resolution. There used to be a federal censor in charge of this work. He was the man who typed the code and told them what they could do. Often during the war the censor prevented certain information from being given out in Canada. The information was held back, and even the House of Commons did not know about it. We were told that we could get some information in a secret session, but I did not attend for the reason I gave at that time-that I thought there would be nothing revealed that the Soviet did not know already.
Now they are adding something new. I must say that the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has been obliging in any contacts I have had with him. But this is going to be a political organization, and I am not using the word "political" in any offensive way so far as the minister is concerned. I have a great deal of confidence in the present minister. I had a lot to do with him during the war. I am not using the word in any personal sense, but because every minister of the crown is more or less in politics. The present Minister of Trade and Commerce did a lot of good work during the war, but this new corporation is to have vast powers over the property and equipment of Canadian Marconi Company, Limited, and Cable and Wireless, Limited, used in connection with external communication services. In the words of the resolution, these communication services are to be operated by the new corporation and they are to be co-ordinated with the services of other parts of the commonwealth. There is no definition of the word "co-ordinated". I linked this matter

Overseas Telecommunication Act the other evening with the Statute of Westminster. As you know, some of the former commonwealth countries are now out of the empire-India, Pakistan, Burma, Ceylon. Seven or eight of them are now out of the empire. They do not belong any more; they are separate organizations, so that this resolution will not apply to them.
You will notice that the Minister of Transport can also make rules and regulations for the corporation. A corporation is to be created called the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation. It is to take over certain property and equipment. Without being subject to any censor at all, the minister is going to have the right to make rules and regulations.
I call your attention to another matter about the new code. The resolution reads, "co-ordinated with the services of other parts of the commonwealth." The Statute of Westminster does not apply in the same way to all parts of the commonwealth. For example, sections 6 to 13 of that statute did not apply to New Zealand and Australia until trouble arose about it over the dollar and the pound sterling and so forth. It is just as I said the other evening. Nevertheless the minister will be able to make rules and regulations.
There are other bodies that deal with external communication services. I have mentioned radio. Everybody knows what the radio corporation does. It takes quite a part in handling external communication services. In conjunction with the B.B.C., the C.B.C. has a code, and there is the power to make rules and regulations. I do not know where it is all going to end. In my view the resolution is simply an extension of the separatist policy of autonomy and sovereignty. That is all it amounts to. It is an extension of that principle which has caused so much trouble in the countries of the empire, and we do not know now who is in the empire and who is out of it.
The resolution proposes to co-ordinate the Canadian service with the services of other parts of the commonwealth. There are embassies all over the world. No wonder we are a separate country. We have ambassadors in the countries all over the seven seas, and the old empire is divided. They are all spending money. The hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), in a very witty speech, referred to these ambassadors as "so-called ambassadors", and the then member for Davenport said, "So-called is right."
Now you will have all these ambassadors in the countries all over the seven seas making use of the code. There will be different codes, and you will not know who is in the empire. These ambassadors learn only by


experience. They also have codes for communication in matters of external affairs. They all want to be ahead of the king and the queen in the procession. They are, as the hon. member for Temiscouata said last year, akin to the undertaker who is first in the procession, or the drum major who leads the band in the royal procession.
I fail to see any necessity for such a measure as this at the present time. Ten years after the beginning of the war you want to co-ordinate these services. Part of the resolution reads:
The Minister of Finance with the approval of the governor in council to be authorized to lend, from time to time, moneys to the corporation out of unappropriated moneys of the consolidated revenue fund, for temporary purposes, the aggregate outstanding at any time not to exceed $100,000.
If you ask me, this is a new policy, appropriating $4,500,000 for these services. I can tell you this, it is another form of separation akin to that of autonomy and sovereignty.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I might deal with some of the difficulties that seem to arise in the minds of hon. members. In the statement which I made at the outset, I believe, will be found most of the answers to the questions that have arisen. There appears to be a misapprehension in the minds of some of the members as to what is to be done. It may be that the statement I have prepared was not a clear one. I shall attempt to elaborate.
In the first place, this resolution which precedes the bill for the establishment of the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation is made pursuant to an international convention. I could go into the history of the telecommunication services from 1928 to date, but that would be somewhat lengthy and it already appears in the statement. After 1928 difficulties in connection with telecommunication services arose in the commonwealth countries owing to competition between beam wireless circuits and cable circuits. The handling of messages by beam was far cheaper than those by cable. I believe I can put it succinctly when I say that about that time it cost twenty-five cents per word to send a message by cable, whereas it cost eighteen cents to send it by beam.
One or the other of these companies was going out of business. So the United Kingdom decided that the best thing to do was to form a merger company. That led to dissatisfaction among certain of the commonwealth countries, so they convened at a number of international conferences, one in 1942 in Australia, where the commonwealth communications council was set up, and that met in 1944. In 1945 Lord Reith, of the United Kingdom government, came to Canada and other commonwealth countries to survey the position and to ascertain what were the views in the various commonwealth countries. In the same year a commonwealth
3S4

Overseas Telecommunication Act telecommunications conference was called in London, and it was there that an agreement was made to which this country and the other commonwealth countries, namely Australia, New Zealand, India, Southern Rhodesia and the United Kingdom, became signatories. The agreement provided two things: (1) that the commonwealth countries should, just as quickly as it is possible to do so, nationalize the telecommunication services within their own territories; and (2) that there should be established what was known as a commonwealth telecommunications board which would act as an advisory board to the various commonwealth countries and co-ordinate the telecommunication services. At an international commonwealth telecommunications conference in 1945 we agreed to do this. We signed the agreement.
While this legislation seems to have been a matter of some surprise to one hon. member, I think it was mentioned not only in the speech from the throne of this session but also in the speech from the throne in the previous session of 1949. I therefore do not think there is a great deal to be said in favour of anyone's being taken by surprise any more than one is taken by surprise when a matter is brought before the house on the first occasion.
I realize that this is a matter of great technicality. While the hon. member for Calgary West says that he does not understand a great deal about it, I can assure him that it is not an easy matter to understand. I do not understand all the things that I should like to understand about it because many parts of it are highly technical and are not very readily comprehensible. As 1 go along, however, I shall attempt to clarify things as much as I can for the committee.
To come back to the apprehension which seems to be in the minds of the members, that this is a lemon that we are taking over, may I say in the first place that the resolution proposes to take over the assets of Cable and Wireless, Limited, and to take over the telecommunication assets of Canadian Marconi Company. The assets which it is proposed to take over are a wireless receiving station at Yamachiche, Quebec, a wireless transmitting station at Drum-mondville, Quebec, together with the Marconi building in the city of Montreal. That has nothing to do with the broadcasting stations of the Canadian Marconi Company; it has nothing to do with the industrial or manufacturing end of the Canadian Marconi Company; nor has it anything to do with the overdraft which was mentioned. This is not a lemon which is being bought. On the contrary, these are assets that have value.


I am informed that the telecommunications end of Canadian Marconi have shown, for the year 1948, a profit of approximately $100,000.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to call the attention of the committee to certain features in connection with this resolution. In the first place it is said that some Conservatives in England approve of this policy. I can say there is a large body of public opinion that does not approve of such a drastic change as this.
We used to have an empire parliamentary association which was set up for the purpose of considering just such matters as this, involving unity within the empire. However they have forgotten all about the empire. They even want to change their name and turn themselves into something else. I believe they turned themselves into a PanAmerican organization. That is one organization to which matters of this kind should be sent, because it is supposed to be nonpolitical. It is the only place I know of where politics are forgotten for the good of the empire and the parliamentary institutions within the empire.
They held a meeting, and we saw what happened to it. Right Hon. Vincent Massey always opposed Pan-Americanism. I admit there are some Conservatives in the Old Country who support this program, but I am

r
absolutely opposed to it for the following reasons-and I shall take only a few moments of the time of the committee.
I was one of the members on this side of the house who, alone, opposed something which I thought would lead just to this new feature and this new program. What was that policy? It was called the Bretton Woods agreement and the monetary fund, which did more to cause disunity the world over than anything else I know of. I was the only Conservative on this side of the house who opposed that agreement-and I am very glad I did.
We have seen the consequences of it-this process of linking up with the international bank, as a result of which one country becomes forever the creditor of all the rest of the world. I was one who opposed it because of that feature in it.
Then, this summer we read about a meeting held near Orillia, on lake Couchiching. Was there any talk about empire up there? No. In fact, hardly any of the countries represented there are in the empire at the present time. Some of them have pledged themselves to a code. But Burma and other places are all out of it. That organization has done more than any other agency I know of to harm the empire. They even wanted to call it something else-to strike out the word "empire", and to call it by some high-sounding name such as "commonwealth". I believe it is now to be called the commonwealth organization, if you please.
The representative from Australia said that it had not been changed by any country within the empire or commonwealth. There was no evidence of it. In fact, I see no evidence of unity right here in the House of Commons. If we read what is proposed about unity within the empire, we find very little of it. The other night I read out a list of nine or ten such things, as they appeared in the debates and order papers of last session, and from the order papers of this session. Was there talk of unity? I say no.
This organization has held its meeting near Orillia. Well, if you ask me I will say this: I do not believe that, at a time when houses are needed so badly for the working-class people of this country, we should bother about these secondary matters. We should attend to primary matters-the ones we are now discussing are only secondary, in my opinion.
We have a large organization at Lake Success known as the United Nations. Up to date I think it would be far better if the name of that lake were changed to Lake Failure-because Russia knows everything that goes on there. They know all about everything. I can tell you that they know
Overseas Telecommunication Act more than we do right here in the House of Commons-and certainly more than we are told.
Is this Orillia organization going to lead to unity within the empire? No. The United Nations tore down buildings worth millions of dollars. They have asked for a code-a code for what? I fail to see any value in this so-called code; there is no unity in it. It is just a waste of public funds. Just wait until you see them next year; it will be a regular sinkhole for capital and maintenance.
And what control have we? Just yesterday we were presented with estimates, but we have no control over them. We pass estimates for this, that and the other thing; but post mortems are all we can ever hold. The people-of this country are worried about what Is becoming of our parliamentary institutions. The tremendous popularity of the monarchy was apparent everywhere in their 1939 visit. The peoples of the empire support the king and queen today, but we see a threat to the dignity of parliament, and we see the decline of the House of Commons, when we hand over all our rights and privileges to these outside organizations such as the one here proposed. Wait until you see the codes which issue from it.
They all make rules and regulations. We have all sorts of organizations, radio, and all the rest of them. I fail to see any value in this proposal, and I venture to say that in the days to come it will prove what I have said when we were discussing the Bretton Woods-, agreement and the international monetary fund. This bill is a simple one, consisting in the main of procedural amendments. Clause 1 provides a new and simplified statement on one part of the exclusive original jurisdiction of the court which is now covered by section 18 of the act. There is no change in substance. Clause 2 provides a simplified procedure on appeal. There are only two new items, of which the first provides for appeal from interlocutory judgment and the second extends from thirty to sixty days the time in which an appeal may be lodged. Clause 3 provides that when an appeal is made on behalf of the crown, the usual deposit of $50 is not necessary. Clause 4 empowers the judges of the exchequer court to make rules and orders for regulating the practice and procedure of and in the exchequer court, as formerly, and adds two new subsections to provide:	(1) for rules dealing with the
examination for discovery in proceedings to which the crown is a party; and (2) for rules providing for the medical examination of a person in respect of whose injury a claim is made before the exchequer court.

I am informed that the judges of the exchequer court have already made rules of this sort, but that there has been some question as to their right to do so. The purpose of this particular clause is to remove any doubt upon the point. I believe the judges have also made one or two orders about medical examination of a person in a case of this kind. Some doubt also exists as to their right to do that. It is to remove that doubt that this clause is introduced.

speechtext: In reply to my hon. friend's question, may I say that I think no substantial injustice is done to anyone under the procedure which is followed by this government in respect of these claims. I would say that over ninety-nine per cent of the claims made against the government are those which arise in cases of negligence. That is one form of tort. Other torts, if indeed there are any others, are quite insignificant in number. In case of negligence I think the procedure that we follow is not without advantage to the subject, for this reason. When the claim is made and a fiat is requested, we have the claim investigated. In the course of that investigation we discover whether, in the opinion of our law officers, the applicant for the fiat has or has not a case against the crown. The judgment arrived at in that regard is the same type of judgment as that which would be arrived at by a lawyer advising an ordinary citizen against whom such a damage claim was made. Where the advantage of applying for the flat comes in is that, in many of these cases, we are able by reason of that inquiry to arrive at a settlement before any damage action at all is started.

No. The application is made. We investigate the occurrence. We decide whether, in our opinion, the claim is a good one or not. If the claim is a good one, we endeavour to make a settlement that is fair before there is any litigation at all. In all those cases the applicant for the fiat is saved what otherwise would have been the costs of starting a case unnecessarily if he were able to launch it without any further difficulty.
What about the cases in which, in the opinion of the law officers of the crown, the applicant for the fiat has no case at all? I grant at once that if, in those cases, we refused a fiat, our position would be an unreasonable one. But the practice is such that, no matter whether we think there is no case or whether we think there is a case, the applicant does not suffer. If in our opinion there is a case, we try to make a settlement without litigation. If in our opinion there is absolutely no case for the plaintiff and he has not a leg to stand on, we nevertheless grant the fiat but we express our view that we do not think so much of the case. I think that procedure might be of some benefit to the plaintiff. While I concede at once that in the abstract it seems like an anachronism,

shall I say, that in 1949 we are still following a practice that is fairly ancient, I would point out that, when you analyse the practical aspect of the matter, I do not think any substantial injustice is done. Indeed, it may well be-although I do not allege this as an assertion for which I take any responsibility- that upon balance those suffering damage as a result of the negligence of the crown are, in the mass, better off. In respect of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police activities, which come under my jurisdiction, I know that from time to time I sign cheques in settlement of claims of this sort, where settlement is arrived at without the necessity for any litigation at all. Those cases could not have been investigated before the writ was issued if the person who had the claim could rush into court and file his statement of claim without making an application to the crown for a fiat.
I will admit this in relation to what my hon. friend said about some of the provinces. A great deal depends upon the fairness with which the fiat is granted or refused. Where the fiat, as with us, is granted as a matter of course, after we have made an investigation, whether we have a defence or not, then no substantial injustice accrues. If, on the other hand, the crown, even in a minority of cases, were disposed to hide behind its immunity from liability and refuse a fiat arbitrarily, I will concede that there would be some injustice to the applicant for a fiat. But I assure my hon. friend that is not the case with this government.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext:
May I assure the minister that I accept everything he has said, and that he has given a completely honest view of the practice. May I discuss it on another basis? I am going to give the minister a concrete example where this thing might go completely wrong. I am glad he mentioned the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Let us assume that a citizen had some complaint about the way he was used by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. As we all know, they are enforcing many laws in nearly all the provinces of the Dominion of Canada. We then come down to the minister's department. The minister has one of his employees look into the matter. Through that employee we seek to get justice, some sort of reparation for injuries, whether physical or otherwise. The minister is then put in this difficult position of saying whether

Exchequer Court Act
or not a fiat should be granted to the citizen who was injured or thought he was injured. The minister is then put in what seems to me to be the unenviable position of having to decide whether or not the fiat should be granted. Let us assume that we have another minister whose ideals of the administration of justice do not coincide with those of the present incumbent of that office, and he says, "I am running a good show; I am running this in the best way that I can and I am not going to have any lawsuits against any of my boys." That is just a natural human feeling that any minister may have under these circumstances. Therefore, sir, with the greatest respect I go back to where I started. It is all right to say that this is never done. Why not make it the law that it can never be done?
I intend to go back and answer one or two other points the minister made. He said that we did not want somebody to fly into the courthouse before the department, whatever department it may be, has had time to make some investigation. I have been in this business of law for a long, long time, and I have never known anybody to sue anybody else, seeking some sort of remedy, without first making a demand on him for the remedial action to which he thinks he is entitled. The minister may think that I am conjuring up something that does not happen, but in saying what he said I think that he was probably conjuring up something that, in the life of this profession, I will not say never happens, but has never been known to me to happen.
Suppose I have a bad lawsuit on my hands. What I would do first of all would be to make a big demand hoping that I would sort of overawe the other fellow. Having some doubt about what my client is entitled to, I think that half a loaf is better than no bread, and I make some settlement in that way. My point is this. If the minister is right in saying that a fiat is never withheld, then I come squarely back and ask: If it is never withheld, why have the prohibition at all? If that were done, then I would hope that the provinces might follow the excellent example which would be set by the Minister of Justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext: Hon. members know that I have not been Minister of Justice for long, and therefore my statement that a fiat had never been refused applies only to the period of the past seven or eight months.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext: Generally I think it has been issued.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext:
Anticipating the type of questions that my hon. friend would raise I took the matter up with my deputy, through a

telephone conversation which was recorded. In our department we have an interdepartmental communication system which enables us to exchange instructions of this sort and have a transcript of them. I have the transcript here and this is what my deputy says:
Well, mind you, we are in no difficult position here because we have had this law in force, well, for a great many years by admitting liability, that is, in the sense of granting a fiat for tort.
Then I said:
Even where we think we are not liable?
Oh, yes, oh, yes, we have never refused a fiat for many years.
You could not get anything more categorical than that, because that is not just myself speaking; that is the deputy, and he is speaking of a period under several ministers. In other words, the practice in relation to this discussion with my hon. friend, in which he said that it might depend to some extent upon the judgment and the temperament of the minister who was exercising it, is not to have even the discretion. I have personally signed fiats where the report from the law offices of the crown was to the effect that we had an excellent defence to the case and that they did not think the plaintiff could succeed.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext: The law offices of the crown have been wrong before.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext:
Oh, yes, of course they have, but the point is this. My hon. friend asks, is not that a terrible responsibility in relation to my staff? I do not think so, because the only responsibility that the minister takes is that of saying: Let justice be done, let the courts decide that the plaintiff has a case against the employees of the department or that there is no such case.
To repeat what I said before: If there were any substantial miscarriage of justice as a result of the withholding of this, then I would be the first to admit the validity of my hon. friend's point. But where the practice is not to withhold the fiat, I am sure the practice does result in a large number of settlements before litigation-because, in relation to that, I have signed many cheques for such settlements.
Beyond a certain amount of delay and a certain amount of extra trouble-and one must admit that-there is no substantial miscarriage of justice at all, and no one is denied justice as a result of the practice followed.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext: As hon. members are aware, I am not a lawyer. I understand, however, that no cases can be brought before this court unless they are against the crown. Am I right in that understanding?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext:
No, that is not right. For example, this court deals with patent cases.

If my hon. friend would turn to section 19 of the Exchequer Court Act he would find the duties set out in paragraphs (a), (b), (c), (d), (e), (f), (g), (h) and (i). All these paragraphs deal with different types of jurisdiction the court may exercise.
Then, under sections 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26 and 27, the various jurisdictions of the court are set out, dealing with railroad debts, and so on. The court has a much wider jurisdiction than merely actions against the crown. However, that is one of the important jurisdictions.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext: What would be the position where the crown is partner with another company-let us say an insurance company? Can such action be brought jointly before the exchequer court?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext: Would the hon. member detail a set of facts in respect of which a claim of that kind has arisen?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext: The National Housing Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext: Yes, the National Housing Act. There is a case pending now where the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation are joint partners with the Manufacturers Life Insurance Company. That case was brought before the ordinary courts, and the ruling handed down that the prosecution could not be brought against the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in any court other than the exchequer court.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext: Right.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext: What is the position when the Manufacturers Life Insurance Company is in partnership with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation? Can they both be prosecuted before the exchequer court, or must they be taken separately? My understanding is they cannot be taken separately because the court would not allow that to be done, and said the only place the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation could be prosecuted would be before the exchequer court.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext:
What my hon. friend has said is that action could not be taken against them jointly in the ordinary provincial courts. But that still leaves the question as to whether action might be taken against them jointly in the exchequer court. I suppose it is the answer to that question the hon. member would like me to give at the present time. Unfortunately, I say frankly, I am not able to give it just now. However, I shall get that information, as to whether joint actions of that sort can be brought.
Certainly I would agree that it should be possible either in the provincial court or in the exchequer court to have the rights of the
Exchequer Court Act
parties determined in a single lawsuit; and I think that is the objective my hon. friend has in mind.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext:
I must repeat that I have no knowledge of the operations of the law in this regard, but when an individual such as a home owner under the National Housing Act finds himself in difficulties with the Manufacturers Life Insurance Company and the government, and finds that he must go to court -bearing in mind that his financial position is not strong-he finds himself in the position where the ordinary court rules that it cannot hear the case because a crown corporation is involved. Then, when further advice is obtained, they cannot sue the Manufacturers Life Insurance Company because if they carried it to the exchequer court they could not bring in the insurance company, which is not a crown corporation.
There you find a situation which confronts the individual whose finances are limited. He cannot sue the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation jointly with the Manufacturers Life Insurance Company in the ordinary courts. He cannot sue the insurance company and the mortgage corporation in the exchequer court because the insurance company is a partner.
It seems to me some provision should be made-and I do not know whether this would be the proper place to make it-whereby a crown corporation could be sued jointly with a private company in the ordinary courts. There are two reasons for that: the first is that the ordinary home owner under the National Housing Act may-and this is most problematical-be able to raise the money to press the prosecution in the ordinary courts. Certainly however he could not raise the money required to carry an action to Ottawa so that it might be heard before the exchequer court.
I hesitate to ask my question, because I do not know what the answer will be. I would ask however what the costs would be to the ordinary individual who prosecutes the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation before the exchequer court. I have no doubt that depends upon the length of the case, and upon other matters; but I have in mind an average case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext:
It would depend upon a great many factors. Even if one knew what the tariff was, and the extent of the court costs, I do not believe he could possibly give an intelligent answer to that question. He would have to know the nature of the claim, the number of witnesses called, and all such information.
However, when the hon. member says that it would cost more to prosecute the case in

Exchequer Court Act
Ottawa, I suggest he is overlooking the fact that the exchequer court sits in different parts of Canada. It goes out on circuit. Proceedings can be instituted through Ottawa agents, following which it is not necessary for counsel in, let us say, Calgary or Edmonton or Winnipeg, to attend at Ottawa with their witnesses.
If all the witnesses on both sides of the case are in some city of Canada, the case can be tried there-provided it is one of the cities on the circuit of the exchequer court judges. In that way I should think the costs of prosecuting a case would be substantially the same in the exchequer court as they would be in the supreme court of a province.
I believe the real point in my hon. friend's remarks, if he will permit my saying so, is his suggestion that an amendment is required to the act to make it clear that in a case where a crown corporation, or the crown itself, is involved with a private company such as the Manufacturers Life Insurance Company, it would be possible to bring action against the crown in the exchequer court and in that action to join the private company as a party in such case, where it appears that there is some business connection between the private company and the crown.
This would enable the case to be brought in the exchequer court where, according to the information the hon. member has given, a court has held that it is impossible to bring a case against both party defendants in the provincial court. His point, as I understand it, is that a plaintiff should be able to get redress against both defendants in the same court at one time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext: I believe we could agree on that.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext:
May I thank the minister for the observations he has just made. I would assume that this would be the proper place to make such a change in the act, and I believe it would be most beneficial if the minister would bring down some amendment at this time, so that it might be incorporated in the legislation.
I would join with the hon. member for Calgary West when he objects to the way a fiat is issued by the officers of the minister's department and by the minister himself. The case I have in mind-and it will do no harm to repeat it now-is that of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the Manufacturers Life Insurance Company versus these home owners I have mentioned.
Here was a case where almost every officer of the crown thus far has disclaimed any responsibility whatsoever in the matter. If it is left in the hands of the minister, or the
IMr. Garson.]
hands of the officers who advise him, to decide whether or not a fiat shall be issued, before a prosecution may take place, then it seems to me that that is not a proper position for the minister to find himself in. This would be the time to enact legislation so that if such an action was brought the court itself could decide the merits of the case and not have the Department of Justice decide whether a fiat should be issued.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext: I am not sure whether I have made myself clear to the hon. gentleman. I must apologize to other hon. members because I think I have said about four times that we grant a fiat as a matter of course.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext: But not as a matter of right or as an obligation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext: As a matter of course. In no case is it refused. Once the fiat is granted the case is then proceeded with against the crown in the same way as it would be proceeded with against another subject.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext: But it could be refused?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext: It could be refused. I am sure my hon. friend has been around the halls of parliament long enough to understand that when a settled practice is developed over a number of years in British countries like Canada the subject can depend upon that practice being followed. As I said before, my deputy minister, who has been at his desk for many years, tells me that he does not know of a single case where a fiat was refused.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext: It is because I have been around these halls for over fourteen years that I would rather see it in the resolution.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext: A point arises in my mind out of the remarks of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. Crown companies are entering more and more into the commercial life of the country. Because of their very nature these crown companies must enter into commercial transactions and I think they should be subject to suit in the ordinary way in the provincial courts. It seems to me that this is a matter that should be taken into consideration because there must be an increasing number of cases where the subject wishes to enter suit against crown corporations.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext: That could be taken care of either by a provision here or by a provision in the act of incorporation of the crown company, that the company shall have a right to sue and be sued in the courts.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext: I suggest that the minister take that into consideration in view of the discussion which has taken place.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext: I shall.

I should like to direct the attention of the minister to a rather unusual situation that exists in Newfoundland at the present time and which has existed for some two or three years. As the minister knows, there is a foreign power, a friendly foreign power, occupying part of our country. From time to time actions for negligence and indeed of a more serious character have taken place. I speak from a full personal knowledge of a couple of actions for negligence which were taken against members of the United States forces. An action could not be taken against the United States government.
In the one case a member of the United States forces was carrying out his regular duties when the cause of action occurred. He was taken before our supreme court where he was represented by United States officers from the judge advocate's office. Judgment was obtained against the soldier and formally entered. When it came to trying to collect the judgment we were informed that the United States army would not recognize it and that we would have to go through some claims commission procedure if we wanted to obtain the amount of the judgment. I know of two cases where that has taken place, where the judgment was not satisfied.
I know of another case where a judgment was obtained in the district court and a promise given that it would be recognized. Afterward that promise was disregarded and the plaintiff received no compensation of any kind. I do not know whether I am right in bringing this to the attention of the minister now, but it is certainly a rather extraordinary position of which the minister should be cognizant.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext: Will the minister bring it to his attention?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.

Would the minister clarify something which has arisen in the last couple of days? He has been discussing the type of case that would come before the exchequer court. Yesterday I asked the Minister of Finance a question with regard to taxation. I am not going to read from Hansard because you might not permit me to do so, as that discussion took place on another matter. The minister said that the taxpayer always had
Exchequer Court Act
the opportunity to appeal to the court. At the time I thought he said that the taxpayer always had recourse, and I do not know whether the word used was "recourse" or "court". speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext: There is another instance where I should not be undertaking to reply to a question which could be replied to more properly by the Minister of Finance. If the taxpayer disagrees or dissents from the assessment he has an appeal to this income tax appeal board. If he is dissatisfied with this disposition of the matter, he has an appeal to the courts.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext: That is the exchequer court.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.

speechtext: While we are discussing the question of jurisdiction, may I ask the minister whether there has been further progress in the catching up by the courts with what was apparently a considerable backlog of judgments?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not know if anything was said about section 2 while section 1 was being discussed, but there is one instance where I think hardship might frequently occur. The new section reads:
82. (1) An appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada lies
(a)	from a final judgment or a judgment upon a demurrer or point of law raised by the pleadings, and,

Exchequer Court Act
(b)	with leave of a judge of the Supreme Court of Canada, from an interlocutory judgment . . .
That puts a litigant to a lot of trouble and expense. I do not expect ever to practise in the exchequer court or in any other court again, but it seems to me it puts litigants to a lot of expense to come to Ottawa, or to retain counsel at Ottawa to go before a judge of the Supreme Court of Canada to obtain leave to appeal. In cases where there is a final judgment there is the right to give notice of appeal without obtaining leave.
Subsection 2 of the new section reads:
(2) An appeal under this section shall be brought by serving a notice of appeal on all parties directly affected-
And so on. There seems to be some confusion. You take away the right of appeal without leave from an interlocutory judgment. Then in the general procedure as to how an appeal should be made there is no distinction between the two.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TIME FOR APPEAL TO SUPREME COURT, ETC.
speechtext:
I think what is intended there is that subsection 2 of the new section 82 applies to all cases where there is the right to give notice of appeal. In the case of an appeal from an interlocutory judgment the application would first be to a justice of the Supreme Court of Canada for leave to appeal. When leave to appeal had been granted, then the appellant would serve the usual notice of appeal on the other side.
As to the other point raised by the hon. member, I could agree entirely with him if it were an appeal from an interlocutory judgment of some provincial court; but in this particular case it is from an interlocutory judgment of the exchequer court which, although it goes out on circuit throughout the country, has its headquarters in Ottawa. I suppose there may be occasions when the interlocutory application might be made to a judge of the exchequer court when he was on circuit, but ordinarily I think it would be made by an Ottawa solicitor acting as agent for the party to the judges here. If it was not inconvenient for them to make their interlocutory application in Ottawa and have it disposed of here, then one would not think it would be any more inconvenient for them to go across the street in Ottawa and apply to a supreme court judge for leave to appeal.

I think that the minister should give serious consideration to the matter before the passage of the bill. It might mean that often litigants might not have sufficient funds to retain a lawyer in Ottawa, which would be necessary in practically all cases, unless the judges were on circuit.
