subtopic: WORICS AND UNDERTAKINGS DECLARED TO BE FOR THE GENERAL ADVANTAGE OF CANADA

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, September 29, consideration of the motion of Mr. Stewart (Winnipeg North) for the second reading of Bill No. 5, to declare the meat packing industry works for the general advantage of Canada.

subtopic: WORICS AND UNDERTAKINGS DECLARED TO BE FOR THE GENERAL ADVANTAGE OF CANADA
speechtext: I notice the sponsor of the bill is not in the house.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: WORICS AND UNDERTAKINGS DECLARED TO BE FOR THE GENERAL ADVANTAGE OF CANADA
speechtext: Is that necessary? The hon. member who moved the adjournment of the debate is here.

subtopic: WORICS AND UNDERTAKINGS DECLARED TO BE FOR THE GENERAL ADVANTAGE OF CANADA
speechtext: We shall proceed with the debate.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: WORICS AND UNDERTAKINGS DECLARED TO BE FOR THE GENERAL ADVANTAGE OF CANADA
speechtext:
The bill before the house has been put forward, I am sure, because of the difficulties the meat packing industry has known in the past. I wish to give credit to the sponsor of the bill for his good intentions in bringing such a matter to the attention of the house. The immediate purpose of this proposed legislation is to take away from provincial legislatures all matters pertaining to industrial relations in the meat packing industry and place them under the control of the federal authorities. To that end, the bill proposes to have the meat packing industry declared a work for the general advantage of Canada or of two or more provinces.
In my view the fate of this bill will rest entirely upon the interpretation of this qualification, "works for the general advantage of Canada". After listening to the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) and the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), I have a definite impression, if not a conviction, that both of them are placing a broad interpretation on those words "for the general advantage of Canada." The introductory remarks of the sponsor of the bill, supported by the address delivered by the member for Vancouver East, would justify the introduction of a bill making other industries in Canada works for the general advantage of Canada. In my opinion, this broad interpretation does not give sufficient reason for singling out the meat packing industry.
If I may refer to the last issue of the Canada Year Book, that of 1948-49, I should like to give an illustration of the practical result of this attempt on their part. This latest issue contains a comprehensive table of the principal industries in Canada. It is found at page 566 and contains a listing of the forty most important industries according to the gross value of their products. I should like to mention the ten industries appearing at the top of that list.
The first one is the pulp and paper industry, with 113 establishments; slaughtering and meat packing, 147; non-ferrous metal smelting and refining, 15; saw mills, 6,001; flour and feed mills, 974; butter and cheese, 2,161; electrical apparatus and supplies, 266; petroleum products, 43; automobiles, 9; and clothing, women's factory, 1,108. The gross value of the first in importance of these industries is $527,814,916, while the gross value of the products of the tenth industry is $174,353,223. We can say, therefore, with-
Meat Packing Industry out any fear of contradiction that these ten leading industries in Canada would afford just as good grounds as the meat packing industry for the placing of their industrial relations under the federal authorities.
In order to better appreciate the table I have given, I should like to refer to another table appearing in the same year book at page 572. This table lists the leading industries according to the number of male wage earners employed. On that basis the tenth largest is the slaughtering and meat packing industry, so we find it has given way in importance to shipbuilding and repairs with 58,000 male wage earners; the pulp and paper industry with 36,000; railway rolling stock, 31,000; primary iron and steel, 28,000; aircraft and parts, 37,000; electrical apparatus and supplies, 23,000; machinery, 21,000; bread and other bakery products, 18,000; and miscellaneous chemical products, 26,000. The slaughtering and meat packing industry is listed as having 18,000 wage earners. I may say that those figures in the table I have just mentioned are for the month of peak employment during 1945.
Having regard to these important industries which operate in this country, and to which I have referred, one may ask himself how it is that the sponsor of this bill has drawn the special attention of this house to the meat packing industry. If it is because he considers that food is the main necessity for the ordinary consumer in this country, he might consider the same necessity existing in the matter of the flour and feed mills, the butter and cheese industry, bread and other bakery products, fruit and vegetables, fish curing and processing and so on. Outside of food there are other essential commodities that the ordinary citizen cannot dispense with, such as clothing, certain varieties of personal items, house furnishings, building materials and so on. The interpretation which is given to that particular word in section 53, paragraph (g) of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, which is in terms identical with section 92 of the British North America Act, subsection 10 (c), opens wide the door to the introduction of dozens of other similar bills which would surreptitiously take away from the ambit of the provincial legislatures' power a good number of matters which by our constitution have been left to their exclusive jurisdiction. There would be no way of drawing the line of demarcation after this bill in its present form has been adopted, if it is adopted.
What are the powers of this parliament in regard to this particular bill? Are we authorized to give any favourable consideration to it? To answer that question, I cannot do any better than to refer to the constitution

Meat Packing Industry itself. All the powers possessed by the federal authority derive from section 91 of the constitution, and all the powers possessed by the provincial legislatures derive from section 92. These two sections are the keystones of our system of government, predicated on the principle of division of authority. Section 91 and section 92 are, I would say, the agents of the distribution of all legislative authority and power in this country. They should complete each other and not come in conflict with each other. They should be interpreted in the same spirit that motivated the fathers of confederation when they wanted to build up a country which, though young, would develop to become one of the leading countries in the world. If one is to give to section 92, and more particularly to subsection 10 (c) thereof, an interpretation which would not conflict with section 91 but would complete it, one cannot be satisfied with the application which the sponsor of the bill has made of the words "for the general advantage of Canada" because section 91, which is the source of the federal parliament's powers of legislation, has a preamble which reads as follows:
It shall be lawful for the queen, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons, to make laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada, in relation to all matters not coming within the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces;
and so on.
With regard to this idea of the federal parliament's taking over powers which have not been specifically assigned to it by the constitution, I cannot think of any better reference in the last few years than that of the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act. One may say that the situation was absolutely inevitable at that time, without any possible controversy. I would answer by saying that is true; but, if the situation was more far-reaching or sweeping, the character of the circumstances which were invoked at that time should not be any different from those which should be the basis of similar legislation, such as that now before us. I could not find any better authority to give an outline of the circumstances which brought about the introduction of this special legislation in 1945 than the statement made by the then minister of justice, now Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). When he moved the second reading of that bill he had this to say, as reported at page 2448 of Hansard of 1945:
The adoption of the motion for second reading of the bill will mean two things, two very important things, both matters of principle: one, that in the opinion of this house the circumstances in which Canada as a whole finds herself during this period of transition to normal from the exceptional conditions existing during the war are still such as

to give some matters comprised within the subjects enumerated in section 92 of the British North America Act aspects of such paramount significance as to take them outside the sphere of that section;
Then he went on with his second point, which referred particularly to the powers given to the governor in council. During his address on that occasion he referred to the jurisprudence laid down by the privy council in the Fort Frances case. He gave several quotations from that judgment, and I should like to draw attention to the following:
In the event of war, when the national life may require for its preservation the employment of very exceptional means, the provision of peace, order and good government for the country as a whole may involve effort on behalf of the whole nation, in which the interests of individuals may have to be subordinated to that of the community in a fashion which requires section 91 to be interpreted as providing for such an emergency. The general control of property and civil rights for normal purposes remains with the provincial legislatures. But questions may arise by reason of the special circumstances of the national emergency which concern nothing short of the peace, order and good government of Canada as a whole.
The speaker then continued and gave a dramatic picture of the situation with which the country would be confronted in the event that the legislation would not pass at that time. In passing, I wish to draw my hon. friend's attention to a statement which the then representative of his party, participating in the debate from which I have quoted, made on that occasion. The gentleman to whom I am referring is Mr. Jaenicke, who was then the hon. member for Kindersley, for whom I have always had great admiration. I have always considered him to be an outstanding lawyer in his province, and I am happy to quote the remarks he made on that occasion. This is what he said, as reported at page 2462 of Hansard of November 23, 1945:
The bill before us, however, enables the ministry to legislate and enact substantive law, and, generally speaking, that is intolerable in democracy in ordinary times, the more so under our constitution because the government by such legislation not only takes over the function of parliament but interferes seriously with the powers of our provinces with respect to subjects which are specifically assigned to provincial legislatures. If we were living in ordinary times, we would undoubtedly oppose the passing of such a bill most vigorously.
In my humble opinion, there is no difference in the character of the circumstances which should prevail in the country to allow the federal parliament by a mere act of parliament and under the authority of section 92 subsection 10 (c) to take away from the provinces some of the matters which had been given to them in a very exclusive and explicit way.
Hon. members who sat on the industrial relations committee in 1947 will recall that a doubt arose in the minds of several hon.

members of that committee about the possibility of the committee recommending what was termed a national labour code. It was thought appropriate to invite the Department of Justice to express an opinion on the jurisdiction of the federal parliament over labour matters. On July 3, 1947, Mr. Driedger, senior advisory counsel of the Department of Justice, appeared and made a lengthy statement, giving his comments and conclusions on the jurisprudence of the privy council which would have some bearing on the matter, and these are the final remarks which he made on that occasion:
(c)	Finally, parliament may, in special circumstances, legislate with respect to labour relations under the initial words of s. 91, namely, for the peace, order and good government of Canada. This was done during the war. The Canada Temperance case (1946) A.C. 193 is the most recent decision of the privy council on the authority of parliament to legislate on this ground. Viscount Simon said that the true test must be found in the real subject matter of the legislation; if it is such that it goes beyond local or provincial concern or interests and must from its inherent nature be the concern of the dominion as a whole then it will fall within the competence of the dominion parliament as a matter affecting the peace, order and good government of Canada though it may in another aspect touch on matters especially reserved to the provincial legislature.
These are general principles and there may be difficulty in applying them to particular cases. No exact test has been laid down as to when or in what circumstances a matter goes beyond local or provincial concern but it is clear that some special circumstances must exist. The authorities are against the view that parliament can in normal times cover the whole field of labour relations in Canada. In the Snider case the point was expressly decided and although the doctrine as expounded by Viscount Simon in the Canada Temperance case is somewhat broader than indicated in the Snider case, it is to be noted that nowhere did Viscount Simon suggest that the Snider case was wrongly decided.
And so on. These are the descriptions referred to in the judgment as the circumstances justifying the federal government intervening in the provincial field of legislation: "abnormal circumstances"; "exceptional conditions"; "standard of necessity"; "some extraordinary peril to the national life of Canada"; "highly exceptional"; "epidemic of pestilence"; and so on.
The situation which now exists in the meat packing industry is something which in no reasonable way meets the circumstances which the higher courts of justice have described in a precise way to give rise to the transfer of powers from the legislatures to parliament.
During the war, under P.C. 1003, the meat packing industry was regulated by the federal government in its labour relations. Through the appointment of an industrial inquiry commissioner, or at the later stage in 1946 by the appointment of a controller and seven deputy controllers, a stoppage of work could
Meat Packing Industry be avoided. Yesterday the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) was kind enough to refer to the able and effective assistance which was provided by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) and his officials in the settlement of that industrial dispute and of those which came about during the war years and in the immediate period thereafter. Since the war, jurisdiction over labour matters which did not belong to the federal parliament was returned to the provinces on May 15, 1947. Not long after, in August, 1947, a strike broke out in the meat packing industry which kept idle six plants of Swift Canadian, and shortly afterwards spread to eleven plants of Canada Packers and six plants of Burns and Company. In all, at the peak of the strike 14,150 men were idle and 47 establishments were closed. This strike situation lasted two months. On October 18 the Swift Canadian Company and the united packing-house workers reached a settlement. An agreement was signed granting a ten-cent-an-hour wage increase, and other difficulties were solved. A few days after that, so far as the other plants were concerned the conciliation machinery of the Ontario department of labour was put to work. A provisional settlement was reached which called for an increase of seven cents an hour, with the proviso that the additional wage increase would be submitted to an arbitrator, Mr. C. P. McTague. The matter was finally closed.
Since then, for the past two years, we have had in the meat packing industry a situation which does not warrant any special attention from a legislative body such as ours The constitution absolutely closes the way for this parliament in connection with matters concerning industrial relations in the meat packing industry.
I submit that the situation now, in thai industry, does not justify our interference with it. This bill is predicated upon a situation of the past and the eventuality of further difficulties in the future. But if this is so, there is no reason why the bill should leave aside all the other industries of importance in Canada, which should be regarded as industries for the general advantage of Canada.
The sponsor of the bill may take to himself the credit for having drawn our attention to this matter. He referred particularly to the effectiveness of the federal Department of Labour during the war, and the transitional period thereafter. He has recognized the soundness of our labour code. The introduction of this bill, in itself, is a recognition of the great qualities of our federal legislation relating to labour relations.

Meat Packing Industry

I submit the
remedy for any abnormal situation which may exist in the field of labour relations, or which may develop in the future, should rest with the provinces themselves. They are the authorities, constitutionally, in these matters. I am sure the federal Department of Labour would be only too pleased to offer and to give the kind of co-operation it has given in the past. Does not section 62 of the labour code constitute a clear offer of collaboration in matters where the importance of a dispute in labour relations generally is nation-wide?
In view of the fact that in the immediate future there is to be a consultation between the provincial premiers and the federal authorities on matters touching the constitution, I suggest the wise course would be to let that consultation take place. There will be drawn a more precise line of demarcation between the responsibilities of the legislatures and those of the federal government. A matter such as the one we are discussing tonight, and other similar problems, could be discussed at that time.
I should think that the best way to achieve a reasonable degree of unity in labour relations, or in any other field of equivalent category, is through a process of consultation and co-operation with the provinces. In my submission, to a certain extent this has already been achieved-and achieved to an important extent, if one recalls that our labour code has already served as a model or inspiration for labour legislation in five or six provinces.
I suggest the bill before the house is not within the jurisdiction of this legislative body, and that we should not attempt to do anything which not only would be trespassing upon provincial rights but would be provocative to the provinces, the co-operation of which is so much needed at this time when, after having developed such a wonderful effort in production and in social legislation, our country now ranks among the most important in the world.
I suggest that in the interests of our country we should not attempt to lay the foundations of any further disagreement with the provinces, and that this bill should not be passed.

subtopic: WORICS AND UNDERTAKINGS DECLARED TO BE FOR THE GENERAL ADVANTAGE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall discuss this bill briefly. Ours is a federal constitution. I know that some trade union organizations have some knowledge of the jurisdictional disputes affecting labour organizations. It is my belief that the fathers of confederation

planned better than they knew when they established a federal constitution in Canada.
This bill is predicated upon the assumption of taking over complete jurisdiction in connection with labour disputes and other matters of that kind in Canada. If it is logical- and I am not now discussing the legal aspect of it-to take over this one industry, then it is just as logical to take over all industries. As I have said before in the House of Commons, Canada is not a country in the same sense as are Great Britain, Germany, France, Belgium, Spain or Holland. This is a continent.
My hon. friends smile. Let me say this, in a kindly way, to the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart), that it was sweet music to my ears when he paid tribute to the Department of Labour during the war under the War Measures Act. It will be understood that I have heard different expressions of opinion.
In confirmation of what was said by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith), when he interrupted a short time ago, let me say that I believe the labour legislation of this country compares favourably with any labour legislation under the canopy of heaven. If my hon. friend will wait just a minute he will learn something as he gets older. There is one difference between my hon. friend and myself; I know what I am talking about and he does not.
I think a tribute is due to all parties in this house for having framed our national labour legislation. We went through a stage during the great war when jurisdiction over labour matters was with the federal government. Since that time stronger labour departments have been developed in all the provinces, and in the main the basic principles enunciated in the federal labour legislation have been copied. This legislation has been in operation for two years and I think it should be given a fair trial. I think it has worked reasonably well; it certainly has worked much better than the legislation in force in other countries. In one country in particular strikes are in the offing in some national industries, something that we have not suffered in this country.

There are countries in

Europe where that is not done at the moment, and when certain ideologies come in through the kitchen, freedom goes out the front door.
From the very nature of things the people in British Columbia have a clearer understanding of the economic conditions affecting the large industries in that province. The people in Nova Scotia I believe have a better understanding of the broad industrial problems of that province. You can go on to New Brunswick, Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba and Saskatchewan, where of course there is not much industry.

It is far better to build with candour than it is with cant. I think we in this House of Commons, we in this Dominion of Canada, particularly those of us in the industrial provinces know something about the difficulties and complexities that exist in a practical way between labour and the great industrial structures of this country. I would rather rely on our experience than on the theories of some schoolteacher or some other person. In saying that, I do not intend to be disrespectful of the school-teaching profession, but I am sure that my hon. friends would object if I tried to read a lecture on how to teach children in school. That is not my profession.
I do not say that on proper grounds and in the proper circumstances a valid declaration could not be framed to declare a meatpacking plant to be a work for the general advantage of Canada, but I point out that the express purpose of the declaration in Bill No. 5 is to enable parliament to legislate in matters of labour relations in the meat packing industry. In effect it is an attempt to do indirectly what parliament cannot do directly, since labour relations fall under
Meat Packing Industry the heading of civil rights and are, therefore, within provincial jurisdiction. The advice that I have from the officers of the Department of Justice is that the declaration as proposed and framed in this bill is open to very serious objections as to its validity.
However, even if the legislation were valid, and even though I were in agreement with the views of the member who has proposed this bill, that the meat packing industry should in the matter of labour relations be under the jurisdiction of parliament, I would still vote against the bill as being the wrong method of procedure to achieve the desired purpose.

There is no equivocation about it. There is in principle nothing to prevent the extension of the principle which it is proposed to apply to the meat packing industry in this bill to any other industry where there are establishments in more than one province, as, for example, departmental-store chains and mail order businesses of all kinds. If a man were fortunate enough to own a hotel in Ottawa and one in Hull he would naturally come under the jurisdiction, as would Canadian Industries Limited which have various types of industrial establishments in a number of provinces.
The device certainly provides a very easy method of procedure for the redistribution of the respective powers assigned to parliament and to the provincial legislatures by the British North America Act. I should think it is quite apparent that legislation of the type illustrated by Bill No. 5 would be regarded by the provinces as an unwarranted invasion of provincial rights and as an opening wedge and a precedent for unilateral action by parliament, having the same effect as an amendment to the British North America Act.

Even in the case of provinces that might be favourable to the ultimate transfer of jurisdiction, in labour matters in the packing industry, from the provincial to the dominion authorities, the procedure proposed in this instance for this purpose would be regarded as objectionable.
I believe therefore that, if and when there is agreement, that jurisdiction in matters relating to labour relations in the meat packing industry should be vested in this parliament, the proper method to follow is by amendment to the British North America Act, as was done prior to the enactment of the unemployment insurance legislation.

I will come to that if you wish. I say to my hon. friend that I am making this speech and I think I know what I am talking about. While there have been a number of instances where specific works have been declared to be for the general advantage of Canada, in any instances involving a substantial number of industrial establishments the purpose was to enable parliament to legislate so as to regulate the management and operation of the industry as a whole as, for example, in the case of grain elevators, which were declared by parliament to be works for the general advantage of Canada. The enactment of the Canada Grain Act, which regulated grain elevator operations, followed upon this declaration.
Reference was made in the debate to the legislation which was passed declaring the Flin Flon works of the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company to be works for the general advantage of Canada, and it was represented that the declaration in that case constituted a precedent for the legislation put forward in Bill No. 5.
The two cases are clearly distinguishable. In the case of the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company operation, the work declared to be a work for the general advantage of Canada was a mine shaft which runs across the interprovincial boundary line between Manitoba and Saskatchewan. As a work connecting two provinces, it was the opinion of the Department of Justice, as I recall it, that this undertaking fell within dominion jurisdiction without the necessity of special legislation. The two provinces concerned, however, desired to have the work declared a work for the general advantage of Canada so as to fortify the assumption of federal jurisdiction.
I should like to say to some of my hon. friends, the jurisdiction of whose provinces is very dear to their hearts, that if we in the federal parliament were to do what the hon. member wants us to do in this one particular instance, I am certain that some of the provinces would object. I am certain if I were a member of one of the provincial legislatures I would object.
I should point out, however, that the declaration in that case was an unqualified declaration. The important distinction, however, is that the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company declaration covered a unique situation, and does not, therefore, establish a precedent. It also had the concurrence of the interested provinces.

Do not overlook the fact that when an industry is brought within the exclusive legislative authority of parliament, workers in the industry lose the benefit of provincial labour legislation regulating wages, hours and conditions of employment enacted for the benefit of industrial workers in provincial industries.
Consequently, in a case such as this one which affects a large number of local plants and a large number of local workers, and in fact the major part of an entire industry, a very strong case must be made for the necessity of the declaration in order to justify it. I do not believe that those who propose this bill will have such a case.
May I say in conclusion that I suppose my department has probably worked in co-operation, and is still doing so, with the provincial governments on more matters than any other department of the federal government. I think if there had been a serious disagreement on policy we would have heard something about it in the House of Commons. 1 can say in all sincerity, I know that my personal relations as minister with every province in the Dominion of Canada have been excellent. I hope they will continue so, and I hope I will not be charged with the responsibility of saying to them, in contravention of the B.N.A. Act, that we are endeavouring to take away from them jurisdiction which belongs to them. I hope that when the house votes on this measure it will agree accordingly.

point in the estimates. Hon. members opposite spent an hour discussing matters connected with meat packing, and it should be a comparatively simple transition now to discuss the matter of meat wrapping.
The other day a distinguished visitor expressed himself as being amazed at the pains we take to wrap meat in what he considered fancy packages. He was astonished that under the present condition of the high cost of living we should spend our money in that way rather than spending it on more of the material wrapped. I wonder whether we as consumers actually insist upon these fancy wrappings, or whether they are forced upon us?
It was by sheer accident that only this morning I happened to pick up the report of a questionnaire and the answers thereto sent out by, I presume, a body of women, known as the Canadian Association of Consumers. They circularized their members with questions in regard to this particular matter, and the answers are interesting. Some of them maintained-and I suggest that some department of government should take note of this -that it was impossible to buy many products in other than these so-called fancy packages in their particular districts. The answers mentioned several commodities, emphasized the needless expense involved in fancy wrappings of certain items, and mentioned in particular some of the lithographing appearing on these wrappings.
But, sir, there are some marketing practices which are perhaps even questionable. Before the cost of foods became so high, certain vegetables and fruits were put out in 20-ounce cans. It was discovered however that with the high cost of living the average family found that these items were somewhat expensive. The result was that the manufacturers produced a 15-ounce can, these being placed on the shelves currently with the 20-ounce can.
The difficulty however was that after a while the 20-ounce can began to disappear, and it was discovered that the 15-ounce can became the regular item available for purchase. But somehow or other, the price of the 15-ounce can began to approach the price of the 20-ounce can, with the result that we have the substitution of 15 ounces of food for what was formerly 20 ounces, but at the same price.
This reminds me of the days when I was homesteading. I remember the transitional period between the five-pound tin of jam which eventually turned into a four-pound tin of jam, but at exactly the same price charged for the larger can. This is an old device.

This matter of packaging may be a small thing to bring up in parliament; but after all we come in contact with these small things in our daily lives and in our housekeeping arrangements. These matters have some importance to us in the House of Commons who represent the people, and particularly the housewives of this country.
The hon. member for Fraser Valley is no1 in his seat, but hon. members will recall the agitation which developed and the great joy taken by the hon. member for Fraser Valley in pointing out the miserable, little green anc worm-eaten peaches with which Ontario hac been afflicted in that particular season. Lei me say to the hon. member who provided us a few days ago with some very fine peaches that there was no condition like that this year.
On that occasion the hon. member foi Fraser Valley protested against the glamorizing of those hard and unpalatable peaches by the use of pink gauze, which made then look rather attractive, and resulted in then being purchased readily, but were the source of great disappointment when the frur reached the buyer's home.
I understand that the use of deceptive devices of that sort, and in particular tha' type of netting, was declared illegal-and ir my opinion properly so. I do not know by what process, whether it was by a dominior or a provincial law.
At previous sessions the minister and ] have had occasional arguments about the quality of Canadian bacon. Tonight I intenc to talk for a few moments about the wrapping on that same bacon. I was surprisec the other morning when, after someone hac bought a package of bacon-I was going te say at our house, but we have never had i house or a dwelling of any sort since cominj here, although we still do have bacon-we discovered this peculiar wrapping.
I notice the minister is looking toward me and I am sure he would imagine that wha I now hold in my hand is a nice, clean piece of back bacon. May I inform him that i is no such thing. When it is sold in slicec form bacon is wrapped in cellophane. I this were a nice, clear piece of cellophane through which one could see clearly, I woulc have no complaint to make about it. It is ; sanitary packaging, even if it is costly.
Formerly packaged bacon was wrapped ii clear cellophane. It was noticed, however that in the packaged bacon the slices were laid in the package so that the lean showee and the fat did not show. The fat showee on the last slice-but there has to be a las slice of everything. Otherwise one woult think that it was all lean. However wher it is opened up, and you are prepared t<

:ry it, you find that you are buying lard at .he same price as you expect to pay for lean neat. Now they have thought up this new lodge, and I think they have crossed the oorderline between honesty and deceit.
I do not know whether the practice is uni-/ersal, but I can say that in respect of the ;wo brands we have purchased-and this me I hold in my hand is Maple Leaf brand, :rom Canada Packers-the bacon is now wrapped in cellophane with red lines on it. This bacon is wrapped in cellophane on which i series of red lines are printed. From across :he counter it makes bacon look pinker and perhaps encourages the customer to buy, Decause he thinks he is buying lean bacon.
[ suggest that it might be a device to cover ip the fatness of the bacon in the package.
[ do not know whether there has been any change in the quality since this device has Deen adopted. When you see a package of .his bacon you might think you were getting i bit of Irish bacon, that nice bacon with alternate strips of lean and fat. In my opinion ;hat result is obtained only by the farmer who keeps one pig that is fed preferably on outtermilk and potatoes, corn meal and table scraps. They have never been able to achieve that result when hogs are fed in quantity. They are generally fed too much grain and too little of other things.
Having talked a bit about bacon, I shall come back to the package. I shall conclude my argument by submitting that this type Df package should be prohibited by law in that it is deceptive. When I picked up this morning the questionnaire I mentioned, I was surprised to find that this very subject had been dealt with. I did not know that these ladies had taken cognizance of this matter. At the bottom of this particular pamphlet put out by the Canadian Association of Consumers I find set out the answers received to questions asked in connection with this very thing. One question was:

In so far as cans are concerned I think there used to be 145 different sizes and forms. Through agreement and regulation this number has been reduced to about 40. This was not done for the purpose of increasing the cost; it was done for the purpose of lowering the cost.
I realize that one can say that for a period of time the price of meat has been going up, but the fact is that the price of meat has been going up constantly since 1938. However, I do notice that often it is in these wrapped packages and I notice also that that is true right across the country. I suppose those who have the product for sale are trying to put it up in the form in which people are most likely to buy it. If somebody in Canada Packers has made a mistake in the type of package they are using, if it does not suit the public, then I presume it will not be very long until Burns or Swifts will find that out and put out some other form of package. There is very little bacon crossing even the provincial boundaries at the

present time as most of the bacon produced is consumed in the province where it is produced. Therefore the control would be entirely with the provinces.

I do not know whether or not the house will permit me to put this 
table on Hansard, but I will indicate what the purport of it is, and if it is desired to have it on Hansard that can be done. I think it will at least refute some of the suggestions that are made in asking for certain information.
The Department of Agriculture is concerned of course in seeing to it that all of the produce of the farms is sold. We are not so much concerned whether it is sold in the West Indies or whether it is sold somewhere else, but we are concerned that it all be sold. I should like to place on Hansard a table which I compiled this afternoon from much more complete records I have here, but which would take far too much space in Hansard. I should like to indicate just what the position has been. I have purposely left out of this table all of the years except 1938, 1944 and 1948. I stopped with 1948 because that is the last year for which we have information. I have had to take 1947 as to apples and potatoes, and also with regard to some items of honey, because complete records for 1948 were not provided to me for those products.
By way of illustration, let us begin with one of the grains that all farmers are concerned with, oats. If I were to take wheat -I have wheat in the table and it will be there if the complete table is put on Hansard- it would not concern so many farmers as oats does. The production of oats in Canada in 1938 was 371 million bushels. In 1944 the production was 500 million bushels, and in 1948 was 358 million bushels. The year 1948 was not a good crop year in many parts of Canada, but the margin between 1938 and 1948 is not very great, 371 million in 1938 and 358 million in 1948.
As to barley, production in 1938 was 102 million, in 1944, 195 million, and in 1948, 155 million. In other words, barley production has risen considerably, and that is partly because the acreage is up.
The domestic disappearance of oats in 1938 was 332 million bushels; in 1944, 424 million bushels; and in 1948, 325 million bushels, just 7 million bushels difference between 1938 and 1948. The figures with regard to barley are 81 million, 172 million and 136 million.
In those figures as to the production and consumption of grains I have omitted the years 1942 and 1943 because we were paying farmers to do certain things with regard to those grains and the figures would be much higher than the figures I have used here for
1944.
Taking exports, we exported 13 million bushels of oats in 1938, 86 million bushels in 1944, and 23 million bushels in 1948. For barley the figures are similar, but if I am

permitted to do so I will put the whole table on Hansard and then I will not need to read all these figures. So far as oats are concerned, we had a carryover of oats at the end of the year 1938 of 49 million, at the end of the year 1944 of 98 million and at the end of the year 1948 of 58 million. The set of figures that refers to oats and barley has to do with grains that are used to feed other products.
When we come to beef we find that in 1938 the production was 588 million pounds; in 1944, 924 million pounds; and in 1948, 891 million pounds. Taking domestic disappearance, consumption of beef, it was 563 million pounds in 1938, 785 million pounds in 1944, and still remains at 734 million pounds in 1948. It was considerably over 800 million in 1947, the year before.
As to pork products, production in 1938 was 646 million pounds; in 1944, 1,737 million; and in 1948 it is still 1,046 million pounds. That is as against 646 million pounds in the year before the war; and for the last year for which we have figures it is 1,046 million pounds. When you come to home consumption, it was 483 million pounds in 1938; 1,056 million pounds in 1944, even in the middle of the war, away above what it was before, and even higher than it is now. It was 839 million pounds in 1948, which is very close to double what it was in the years preceding the war. We are consuming the pork in this country.
Our exports of pork products in 1938 were 178 million pounds; in 1944, 717 million pounds; and in 1948, 226 million pounds. Our exports were still higher in 1948 than they were in 1938 by a considerable margin. We had a carryover of 27 million at the end of the year in 1938, 49 million in 1944, and 16 million in 1948.
I do not think it is necessary for me to read any of the other figures if I am permitted to put the whole table on Hansard. I have here butter, cheese, poultry, eggs, apples and other products. There is a very interesting thing about apples. When you look at these figures you find that our production of apples in 1938 was 15-6 million; in 1944 it was 17-8 million; and the production in 1947, which is the last year for which I have a record, was 15 -6 million. The production for 1948 was a little over 13 million.
Let us take domestic disappearance, which is the important factor in connection with apples. In round figures the disappearance in Canada, that is, the marketing of apples in Canada, was 7 million bushels in 1938, 12 million bushels in 1944 and 14 million bushels in 1947. In other words, there were twice as many apples marketed in Canada in 1947 as there were in 1938. I have always understood the problem in connection with

The same thing is not going to happen this year as happened some years ago when other governments dealt with oleomargarine. We have seen to that. A floor price has been put under butter. I am not going any further into the matter than to say the same thing did not happen this year with regard to butter as happened when oleomargarine was brought in before. At that time butter was up, as I recall it-and I am speaking from memory now-around 70 cents a pound, and before they got through with the experiment it was down in the twenties. This time butter was held up around 70 cents a pound when oleomargarine was introduced; and there is no doubt in my mind that, if the government had done nothing about it, butter would again have gone down to at least 40 cents and might have gone down further. But the government put a floor under it and kept it at 58 cents during the summer. The policy that is being followed is one of stabilizing the price; it is not one of holding the price up to the consumer but one of stabilizing the price at around 58 cents. The government has some 46 million or 47 million pounds of butter in its possession in order to see to it that no one charges an outrageous price for butter between now and next spring, when our cows go out on the grass again to produce butter in great quantity. In other words, there is some regulation upon it. While the farmer benefited during the summer months by the fact that the price did not run down, the consumer will benefit during the winter months by the fact that it will not run away up out of all proportion to what it should be.
To answer the other part of the question, as to what difference oleomargarine has made, I am not too sure. Last spring everybody was telling me that no one knew the 45781-28
Supply-Agriculture
difference between oleomargarine and butter, but along in the middle of the summer oleomargarine went down from something over 40 cents to around 30 cents, while butter was holding at 58 cents. Some people must have known something about it.
I was just telling someone across the floor tonight that I had something to do with a massive Great Dane dog that was fond of butter. His mistress gave him bread with butter spread thickly on it; but being Scotch, she came to the conclusion that there was no use spending so much money, so she went and got a pound of oleomargarine and spread the bread with it. The dog sniffed at it, put his tail between his legs and went and lay down in a corner as far away as he could get from it. In other words, if individuals do not know the difference between butter and oleomargarine, dogs do.
I do not know whether or not oleomargarine is entirely responsible for the lower consumption recently; but the consumption of butter during the last few months, as compared with the months immediately preceding, is down about 3 million pounds. That does not get it down to the long-term average, but it is down by 3 million pounds. That is shown by the records that we are able to compile. Our records are confined to the storages, and are based upon the records in a number of cities across Canada. But everyone in this committee knows that today there is a great deal of butter stored in freezers all over the country; and I am not so sure that the 3 million pounds that is indicated as the reduction, on the general statistics as we have compiled them over the years, indicates the true picture. There is a possibility that the consumption is not down as much as has been suggested by the figures I have given. But the outside figure in any case is 3 million pounds down in the last few months as compared with those immediately preceding.

Is the price of butter pegged in Canada, and what is that price? I ask this
[Mr. Fulton. 1
question because I understand something was mentioned a moment ago about the price of butter in Newfoundland being eight-five cents retail per pound. I know it was eighty-five cents before the union, but the retail price is now seventy-five cents. I am asking this question because, if I am given the pegged price, I can figure out exactly what the price should be in Newfoundland, and find out if some of our people down there are charging us too much.

subtopic: WORICS AND UNDERTAKINGS DECLARED TO BE FOR THE GENERAL ADVANTAGE OF CANADA
speechtext:
There is no pegged price, but there is a floor price. Last spring we said that for a twelve month period we would take delivery of butter at 58 cents a pound, grade A. If anyone else wanted to get the butter he had to pay at least 58 cents for it. They might in some cases have to pay a little more than that; but they would have to pay at least 58 cents, because we were on the market all the time to take it at 58 cents. We had about 46 million or 47 million pounds of butter, and we will probably have a little more before the winter season comes on. Everyone else who has butter has about half that amount, or not quite half that amount.
We are in a position of holding that butter. If anyone is selling butter at 75 cents where he should be charging only 65 cents for it, some trader there will find that out and will apply to the government for butter. If he gets butter from us under the policy we are following it will be at 58 cents, plus the freight to the point to which it has to go, and all other costs of setting it down in that place. This leaves us with our return of 58 cents, grade A butter. The butter will be regraded and put out at its proper grade and at whatever the price is in relation to 58 cents.
Just stating what I would do if I were doing it-they usually ask me about these things-if we found that a certain individual, after getting butter down there, could retail it and get the same profit as men are getting elsewhere across Canada by selling it at 65 cents, let us say, and if he were selling it at 75 cents, he would not get any more butter from the board. The butter would go to those who were selling at reasonable prices to the consumer.
If butter is out of line in Newfoundland, we will be looking very shortly for places to put our surplus butter when it comes in, and we will look to Newfoundland as well as to other places.

I should like to ask a question or two in connection with the hog industry. At the present time there is a certain amount of perturbation in the minds of people engaged in the production of hogs as to just what the situation is likely to be in the coming year. This feeling of alarm arises from several factors.
First of all there is the matter of the devaluation of the British pound. As everyone familiar with the hog industry knows, for some considerable time we have had in Great Britain a market for our surplus bacon. In other words, they have taken the surplus of our pork products above what we consumed ourselves. During the last year a floor price had been in effect under hogs, owing to the existence of the British contract.
The question in the minds of a large number of producers of hogs is whether that contract can be renewed on anything like the terms we have had in the past, or whether the devaluation of the British pound is going to make it impossible for us to sell our bacon to Great Britain in competition with that from soft-currency countries?
Allied with that, of course, is the fact that in the past year we have not come anywhere near meeting our contract with Great Britain for bacon. The contract is for 160 million pounds. I notice in this publication put out by the department, dealing with the livestock and meat trade, it is stated, in the issue for September 22, that the total amount of bacon sent to Great Britain up to September 17 of this year was just over 25 million pounds. Only three months of the year are left, and it is quite clear that we are not going to come even close to meeting our contract.
The thought in my mind, and in the minds of many producers, is what effect this will have upon our ability to get another contract. Naturally, when one enters into a contract and does not fulfil it, there is bound to be a certain amount of wonder as to whether or not another contract will be offered. Therefore this is a natural fear. The fact that we have not made our contract is certainly not the fault of the people engaged at this time in the production of hogs. It is due to other factors I have discussed with
Supply-Agriculture
the minister at various times, and the basis of which I shall not go into at the moment.
There is another factor which adds to the alarm, namely the large corn crop in the United States, and the fact that their pig crop in that country is greater than it has been normally. The probability is that the price of pork will drop in that country owing to the over-supply of feed, and that will likely make available a considerable amount of pork and pork products for export. Of course, that is bound to affect those overseas markets in which our pork might be sold. I should like the minister, so far as he can, to outline to the committee and to the country at large what the situation is likely to be or what the government estimates it is likely to be in 1950 as far as hogs are concerned.
I should like the minister to tell us to what extent production in this country is down. The department has very good figures, some of which they put out from time to time, and I think the minister would be in position to tell us what the departmental estimate is for hog production during the first six months of 1950. It may be that on the basis of that estimate we will not be producing any more pork than we can consume in Canada and therefore the fears entertained by the hog producers will be considerably allayed.

speechtext:
Current marketings are
running a little ahead of last year; they have been increasing week by week for some time over the marketings of a year ago. At the moment production is on the upward march and the estimate is that that will continue. We do not think that production will be lower in the first six months of 1950 than it was in the first six months of 1949.
Coming to the other question of what effect our deliveries may have upon the British market, I can only say what I said during the last session, namely, that when the British came here about two years ago they did not want any bacon; they did not want any of our products except wheat. For anyone to say that there is any reason for disappointment in Britain because we did not deliver any of these products is to fail to take into consideration the facts of the case.
The British said two years ago, "We have not the dollars with which to buy anything but wheat." Then a year ago they took the position that they only had dollars with which to buy wheat and cheese. We said to them at the time, "We do not think it is a good thing, either for our people or for your people, to drop these agreements just because you have not the dollars. We think it would be much more to the advantage of both of us if we did enter into contracts."

Supply-Agriculture
We gave them a definite undertaking at the time that we would try to hold our contracts down to realities.
In the years during the war and immediately before the war we were writing into the contracts more than we anticipated our farmers would be able to produce. In other words, we were trying to increase production because Britain required the bacon during the early part of the war. When it would be suggested that so many million pounds be put into the contract we added another fifty million pounds and said to everybody, "Go out and produce it." Our farmers produced it, and more on top of it.
When we got down to the latter part of the war, when Britain wanted grain instead of meat products, we did not say to the farmers, "Do not produce hogs as you produced them before." But apparently, looking at the records that were coming over the radio and from Great Britain in one way or another, those farmers who wanted to grow grain particularly, and there are farmers in the west who have always been accustomed to producing grain and who like to grow grain better than anything else, finding they could make more money doing that, or could make some profit thereby-we were not urging them to produce more hogs, because the British had already told us they did not want to buy them-were told to go ahead and do the thing they felt they were best equipped to do and which they wanted to do.
The result has been as I indicated by the figures I gave a few minutes ago. They are producing more hogs than they produced before the war, but our people are eating around seventy per cent more pork products than they did before the war. The result of those two things leaves us with less pork products to send to Britain than we have sent over a long term of years.
We have said to the British, "We have always met your contention that you do not want to buy bacon. We have almost made it unnecessary for you to put up dollars to buy bacon, but some day this thing is going to turn". It has turned already with cheese. We got the quantities down in the cheese contracts to a figure of 50 million pounds. When we wrote that figure into the contract we did not think we would be able to fill it, neither did the British. But the price of canned milk went down and farmers switched over to the production of cheese with the result that we got 60 million pounds which we could have sent to Britain. Then we said to the British, "In view of the fact that you are not getting bacon and do not want to get it, in view of the fact that you were prepared to pay so many dollars for the

bacon, why not take the other 10 million pounds of cheese?" But they would not take it.
All I am suggesting is that there was no lack of understanding with regard to bacon between those who negotiated the contracts. They understood that if we could persuade our own people to eat it at a better price than they were paying for it, or if we could send it to the United States at a better price than they were paying for it, that was quite all right with them; they did not want the bacon. Perhaps I should not say they did not want the bacon; they did not feel that they had enough dollars to be able to buy the bacon. There has not been any misunderstanding created in Britain that would take that market away from us. We have said to them that they do not have to pay dollars for products that we can sell for dollars in our own country or in the United States.
Then with regard to next year. I am not in position to report what the British are prepared to do next year with regard to contracts, but I am in position to say that we are insisting in every way we possibly can that we do have a contract on bacon, whether we can deliver it or not. We think it would be a good thing, both for Britain and for ourselves, if they were prepared to say, "If you do have a surplus, we are prepared to take at least a certain amount of it". We would like a contract with regard to cheese. I do not think we will have much difficulty getting one in regard to cheese. We would like a contract in regard to eggs.
We would like contracts with regard to the four products, cheese, bacon, eggs and wheat, the four products in connection with which we now have contracts. We are still trying to negotiate contracts for the year that is ahead and for a longer time if we can. That is the position at the present time. I do not think that anything we have done up to date has jeopardized our position in the British market. On the other hand, what we have been doing has got rid of the production of our farms.

I should like to direct a few remarks to the Minister of Agriculture about what may be termed the orphan of the dairy industry. When I was a boy we were always told that Leeds leads in the production of cheese, but through the years our cheese factories have gradually diminished with the advent of milk condenseries. Today we have three milk condenseries looking after 2,250 milk patrons. That is the equivalent of 75 cheese factories, figuring 30 patrons to a factory. At the present time 520 of those patrons who have been going to the condenseries are sending their milk to the cheese factories but this is only a temporary situ-

ation. Apparently the condenseries have cut their production by 20 per cent. In fact they have cut it to such a serious degree that they cannot economically produce evaporated milk. Stocks of evaporated milk have increased enormously. I should like to quote some figures from the bureau of statistics. Last year there were 26,892,000 pounds in storage, and on the first of August of this year there were 55,147,000 pounds in storage. In the county of Leeds alone we have over 8 million pounds in storage. One plant has leased a Canadian Pacific roundhouse; it has it stocked to the roof, and they are still looking for further storage space. When the cold weather comes it is going to be a problem to keep it heated. Another plant has leased an old church, and it is rapidly being filled with milk powder.
I commend the minister for the attitude of his department in bonusing premium cheese, and in buying up supplies of cheese now that we have filled the British contract. I commend the minister for maintaining a floor price on butter, and also for purchasing the surplus production of butter, but we are facing a very serious situation in those sections of Canada where condensed milk and evaporated milk are being produced. In the spring, stocks of powdered skim milk were bought up, but this year stocks have increased in one year from 9,130,000 pounds as at September 1, 1948, to 12,162,000 pounds. There are no bonuses and no premiums paid to the producers of evaporated milk, and yet these factories are paying the highest price to their patrons for their milk.
The situation is getting quite desperate. Milk is being sold on world markets at a loss to reduce inventories. Evaporated milk is being sold in Canada today at a loss. The same thing may be said in respect to heavy shipments to Belgium, western Germany and Cuba. The sterling zone of the British empire used to be the biggest market for Canadian producers of evaporated milk. Today that area is buying its milk from Holland and Australia, both being soft-currency countries. Last year Great Britain withdrew orders for 300,000 cases of evaporated milk, which means that not one drop of Canadian evaporated milk has entered the British market in nearly two years. Today evaporated milk producers are facing a loss of markets even in the British West Indies, which has been a constant market since long before the war, and a heavy consumer of Canadian evaporated milk products during the war.
I wish the Minister of Trade and Commerce were here, because I know that to a large extent marketing comes under his department. It seems to me that markets could be found abroad for evaporated milk in
Supply-Agriculture
the central American countries. We could buy their citrus fruits and their coffee and sell them some of our surplus milk. They are tropical countries, and it is hard to produce milk products there. I also suggest that we try to get into certain parts of the empire such as Malaya, India, Pakistan, South Africa and West Africa, and that further negotiations be conducted. I understand that we are going to buy more tin and rubber from Malaya. Could we not buy peanuts from West Africa, and cotton from Egypt? Surely some method can be devised to diminish these stocks which are now becoming a serious problem for all producers of evaporated milk across Canada.
An attempt might be made to increase the domestic use by asking bakers to include a certain amount of evaporated milk powder in their bread. I believe that was done during the war in the standard loaf served to the armed forces. Perhaps we could get rid of a large surplus in the home market. I understand that it makes better-tasting bread and increases its vitamin content.	[DOT]
I repeat that in the county of Leeds alone there are 2,250 farmers dependent on the condenseries for their livelihood, and they are naturally becoming anxious about their future. May I suggest that attention be paid first to finding methods of regaining markets that we have lost, second, to increasing home consumption of evaporated and condensed milk, and skim milk powder, and third, to the purchase of surplus stocks of processed milk products by the government in order to relieve a situation that is now assuming really serious proportions. Farmers producing milk for condenseries in the county of Leeds are becoming so apprehensive that they hardly know which way to turn. They are asking that some course be followed that will assure them of a constant market for their products, because I can imagine no greater calamity befalling the farmers in this great dairying section of Canada than if it were necessary for any of these plants to close their doors.
